questions.q: Why did the victory that day turn into mourning for all the people?
questions.a: The victory turned into mourning because the people heard that the king was grieved because of his son.

questions.q: What was the king’s cry?
questions.a: The king cried, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!”

questions.q: What did Joab say would have pleased the king?
questions.a: Joab said that he could see that if Absalom were still alive and all of David’s men were dead today, David would like that better.

questions.q: What did Joab tell the king would happen if he did not go out and speak to his servants?
questions.a: Joab swore by Yahweh that if the king did not go out, all his soldiers will have abandoned him by tomorrow morning.

questions.q: When did all the people come before the king?
questions.a: All the people came before the king after they were told that the king was sitting in the gate.

questions.q: What were the people in the tribes of Israel arguing about?
questions.a: The people were arguing about what they should do now that Absalom was dead and David had left Israel to escape from Absalom.

questions.q: Whom did King David send to speak to the elders of Judah?
questions.a: David sent Zadok and Abiathar the priests to speak to the elders of Judah.

questions.q: Whom did David say would be the commander of his army in place of Joab?
questions.a: David said Amasa would be the commander of the army in place of Joab.

questions.q: Why did the men of Judah come to Gilgal?
questions.a: The men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring him across the Jordan.

questions.q: Who rushed to the Jordan to meet the king?
questions.a: Shimei, with 1,000 men from Benjamin, and Ziba, with his 15 sons and 20 servants, rushed to the Jordan.

questions.q: Why did Shimei say he was the first from the house of Joseph to meet the king?
questions.a: Shimei came first because he knew that he had sinned against the king.

questions.q: What did the king say to Shimei after Abishai said Shimei should be put to death?
questions.a: The king told Shimei that he would not die, and he swore an oath to him.

questions.q: How did Mephibosheth look when he came to meet the king?
questions.a: Mephibosheth had not cared for his feet, trimmed his mustache, or washed his clothes from the day the king went away.

questions.q: What reason did Mephibosheth give for not going with the king?
questions.a: Mephibosheth told the king that his servant, Ziba, had deceived him and left without him, and Mephibosheth could not follow him because he was crippled.

questions.q: What else did Mephibosheth say Ziba had done to him?
questions.a: Mephibosheth said Ziba had lied about him to the king.

questions.q: How did Mephibosheth reply when the king said he and Ziba should divide the field?
questions.a: Mephibosheth told the king to let Ziba take the whole field, because all that mattered to him was that the king had returned safely.

questions.q: What had Barzillai done for the king?
questions.a: Barzillai had provided all of the food that the king and his soldiers needed while they were at Mahanaim.

questions.q: Why did Barzillai say he should not go to Jerusalem with the king?
questions.a: Barzillai said he was too old, could no longer taste what he ate or drank, could not hear singers, and would be a burden to the king.

questions.q: What did Barzillai request of the king?
questions.a: Barzillai asked to return to his own city to die, but he asked the king to take his servant Chimham and do for him what was good in the king’s eyes.

questions.q: Who crossed over to Gilgal with the king?
questions.a: Chimham, all the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel crossed over to Gilgal with the king.

questions.q: Why did the men of Israel say they had more right to David than the men of Judah?
questions.a: The men of Israel said they had more right to David because they represented ten tribes that were related to the king. The men of Judah represented only one tribe. Also, the people of Judah had started the rebellion against David.

questions.q: Whose words were harsher, the men of Judah or the men of Israel?
questions.a: The word of the men of Judah was harsher than the word of the men of Israel.

commentary.text: Joab causes David to cease mourning.

Verses 1–8 To continue to lament for so bad a son as Absalom, was very unwise, and very unworthy. Joab censures David, but not with proper respect and deference to his sovereign. A plain case may be fairly pleaded with those above us, and they may be reproved for what they do amiss, but it must not be with rudeness and insolence. Yet David took the reproof and the counsel, prudently and mildly. Timely giving way, usually prevents the ill effects of mistaken measures.

God's providence, by the priests' persuasions and Amasa's interest, brought the people to resolve the recall of the king. David stirred not till he received this invitation. Our Lord Jesus will rule in those that invite him to the throne in their hearts, and not till he is invited. He first bows the heart, and makes it willing in the day of his power, then rules in the midst of his enemies, Ps 110:2, 3.

Those who now slight and abuse the Son of David, would be glad to make their peace when he shall come in his glory; but it will be too late. Shimei lost no time. His abuse had been personal, and with the usual right feeling of good men, David could more easily forgive it.

David recalls the forfeiture of Mephibosheth's estate; and he expressed joy for the king's return. A good man contentedly bears his own losses, while he sees Israel in peace, and the Son of David exalted.

Barzillai thought he had done himself honour in doing the king any service. Thus, when the saints shall be called to inherit the kingdom, they will be amazed at the recompence being so very far beyond the service, Mt 25:37. A good man would not go any where to be burdensome; or, will rather be so to his own house than to another's. It is good for all, but especially becomes old people, to think and speak much of dying. The grave is ready for me, let me go and get ready for it.

The men of Israel though themselves despised, and the fiercer words of the men of Judah produced very bad effects. Much evil might be avoided, if men would watch against pride, and remember that a soft answer turneth away wrath. Though we have right and reason on our side, if we speak it with fierceness, God is displeased.
